title: Advances in hybrid hydrogel design for biomedical applications: innovations in drug delivery and tissue engineering for gynecological cancers.

sections.heading: Design and synthesis of hybrid hydrogels
sections.text:
Design and synthesis of hybrid hydrogels Chemical Crosslinking Chemical crosslinking is a critical technique in forming hybrid hydrogels, providing them with necessary structural integrity and functionality for biomedical applications, especially in gynecological cancer treatment. This process contains constructing covalent bonds between polymer chains to obtain a stable and durable network. Various methods and materials are employed to achieve chemical crosslinking, each contributing unique properties to the final hydrogel. One of the most widely used methods for chemically crosslinking hydrogels is free radical polymerization (Salahuddin et al.  2021 ). This technique involves generating free radicals, which initiate the polymerization of monomers to form polymer chains that subsequently crosslink (Moncada et al.  2023 ). Free radicals can be generated using thermal initiators, UV light, or chemical initiators. This method is versatile, permitting the addition of diverse functional groups and nanomaterials into the hydrogel matrix. For example, UV-induced free radical polymerization is often employed to create photo-crosslinked hydrogels with precise control over the network structure and mechanical properties(Wang et al.  2023 ). Additionally, click chemistry represents a highly specific and efficient approach to chemical crosslinking. It involves reactions that form covalent bonds between polymer chains with high yield and under mild conditions. A prominent example is the azide-alkyne cycloaddition, which facilitates the formation of robust hydrogel networks(Wang and Zhang  2022 ; Singh et al.  2022 ). The specificity and efficiency of click chemistry make it particularly appropriate for biomedical field where precise control over the hydrogel's architecture and functionality is required. Enzymatic crosslinking leverages enzymes to catalyze the formation of covalent bonds between polymer chains. This method is advantageous for its biocompatibility and ability to proceed under physiological conditions. For instance, horseradish peroxidase (HRP) can catalyze the crosslinking of phenol-containing polymers within hydrogen peroxide(Chen, et al.  2025 ; Singh, et al.  2025 ). Enzymatic crosslinking is particularly useful for creating hydrogels intended for tissue engineering and regenerative medicine, where maintaining a biological environment is crucial. Notably, various materials are employed in chemical crosslinking to create hydrogels with specific properties (Table  1 ). Polyethylene Glycol (PEG): Known for its biocompatibility, hydrophilicity, and ease of functionalization, PEG-based hydrogels are often crosslinked using methods like free radical polymerization and click chemistry(Dong et al.  2022 ; Kulkarni et al.  2023 ). These approaches facilitate the production of hydrogels with designed mechanical and biological features, making them ideal for drug delivery and tissue engineering(Pagar et al.  2022 ). Alginate: This natural polymer is biocompatible and forms gels within divalent cations. Chemical modifications allow for covalent crosslinking, enhancing the stability and functionality of the hydrogels, making them suitable as biocompatible scaffolds(Lin et al.  2020 ; Simão et al.  2020 ). Chitosan: Derived from chitin, chitosan is frequently used in hydrogel formation due to its biocompatibility and biodegradability. It can be chemically crosslinked using agents like glutaraldehyde or genipin, creating stable networks that are ideal for drug delivery and tissue engineering(Bencherif et al.  2009 ; Tak et al.  2023 ). Polyvinyl Alcohol (PVA): A synthetic polymer distinguished by its capacity to form films, emulsify, and adhere. PVA can be chemically crosslinked with agents such as glutaraldehyde or boric acid, resulting in hydrogels with robust mechanical and physical properties, making them fit for various biomedical settings(Ai et al.  2023 ; Jain et al.  2021 ).
 Table 1 The materials used in chemical crosslinking of hybrid hydrogels for biomedical applications, particularly in gynecological cancer treatment Material Description Crosslinking Methods Applications Reference Polyethylene Glycol (PEG) Synthetic polymer known for biocompatibility and ease of functionalization Free radical polymerization, click chemistry Drug delivery, tissue engineering Dong et al.  2022 ; Kulkarni et al.  2023 ; Pagar et al.  2022 ) Alginate Natural polymer from seaweed, biocompatible, forms gels with divalent cations Chemical modification for covalent crosslinking Biocompatible scaffolds Lin et al.  2020 ; Simão et al.  2020 ) Chitosan Biocompatible polymer derived from chitin, used in stable network formation Glutaraldehyde, genipin Drug delivery, tissue engineering Bencherif et al.  2009 ; Tak et al.  2023 ) Polyvinyl Alcohol (PVA) Synthetic polymer known for film-forming, emulsifying, and adhesive properties Glutaraldehyde, boric acid Robust, durable biomedical materials Ai et al.  2023 ; Jain et al.  2021 ) PEG is a versatile synthetic polymer that forms hydrogels with excellent biocompatibility and hydrophilicity. PEG-based hydrogels can be crosslinked through free radical polymerization or click chemistry, which permits accurate management of the mechanical and biological properties of the hydrogel(Fu et al.  2017 ). This makes PEG hydrogels particularly suitable for applications in drug delivery, where structural integrity and biocompatibility are crucial(Bae et al.  2015 ). Alginate, a natural polymer obtained from seaweed, is widely used in biomedical fields because it can create gels when interacting with divalent cations like calcium(Khanmohammadi et al.  2018 ). This gelation process can be further enhanced by chemical modifications that enable covalent crosslinking, thus improving the hydrogel's stability and functionality. Alginate hydrogels often served as biocompatible scaffolds that promote cell growth and tissue regeneration(Seitz et al.  2024 ). Chitosan, derived from the natural polymer chitin, is known for its biocompatibility and biodegradability. It forms stable hydrogels when chemically crosslinked with agents such as glutaraldehyde or genipin. These crosslinked chitosan hydrogels are particularly effective in drug delivery systems, where they offer a controlled release of therapeutic agents, and in tissue engineering, where they support the formation and repair of tissues(Shi et al.  2023 ). Polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) is a synthetic polymer characterized by its excellent film-forming, emulsifying, and adhesive properties. PVA hydrogels can be formed by chemically crosslinking with agents like glutaraldehyde or boric acid(Ghassemi et al.  2021 ). These hydrogels exhibit robust mechanical and physical characteristics, allowing for a series of biomedical applications, including as durable scaffolds in tissue engineering and matrices in drug delivery. Critical appraisal of crosslinking modalities for clinical-grade hydrogels: Among the various chemistries described above, click‐based strategies—especially strain-promoted azide–alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC)—offer the most compelling path toward GMP-compliant, clinical-grade hydrogel manufacture. SPAAC proceeds with quantitative yields under physiological conditions, avoids cytotoxic catalysts and ultraviolet irradiation, and leaves minimal residual reagents, thereby minimizing immunogenic risk in gynecological tissues. In contrast, conventional free‐radical polymerization (e.g., UV- or thermally-initiated) may generate residual radicals or unreacted photoinitiators that can provoke local inflammation and accelerate unintended degradation in vivo. Enzymatic crosslinking (e.g., horseradish peroxidase/H₂O₂) achieves excellent biocompatibility and precise temporal control but relies on enzyme availability and can suffer batch-to-batch variability—factors that complicate large-scale, standardized production. Impact on degradation, immunogenicity, and drug release: Crosslink density and chemistry govern mesh size, degradation kinetics, and payload diffusion. Highly crosslinked PEG networks (mesh size < 20 nm) provide sustained release over weeks—ideal for peritoneal cisplatin depots in ovarian cancer—whereas lower‐density networks accelerate release for rapid drug delivery to cervical stroma. Importantly, choice of small‐molecule crosslinkers also affects host response: glutaraldehyde–chitosan hydrogels have been associated with macrophage activation and fibrotic encapsulation, whereas genipin‐crosslinked matrices elicit significantly reduced inflammatory cell infiltration in both subcutaneous and vaginal implantation models. This evidence underscores the necessity of selecting crosslinking chemistries not only for mechanical stability but also for predictable degradation, low immunogenicity, and tunable drug release tailored to the unique microenvironments of gynecological tumors. In conclusion, selecting materials and methods for chemical crosslinking is crucial in developing hybrid hydrogels with specific properties tailored for biomedical applications. Each material offers unique advantages, enhancing the effectiveness and capabilities of the hydrogels in drug delivery and tissue engineering, particularly for treating gynecological cancers. Continued advancements in these areas will further expand the potential of hybrid hydrogels in clinical settings. Physical crosslinking Physical crosslinking is a key method for creating hybrid hydrogels, offering benefits like reduced toxicity and the ability to form reversible, stimuli-responsive networks. These interactions help form robust yet flexible hydrogels suitable for various biomedical applications, particularly where dynamic and responsive properties are needed. Here, we explore various physical crosslinking techniques and their benefits in biomedical fields, especially in drug delivery and tissue engineering for gynecological cancers. One prevalent technique in physical crosslinking is ionic interactions (Sood et al.  2023 ). This method employs multivalent ions to bridge polymer chains, creating a gel network. It is commonly used with natural polymers like alginate, which gels within divalent cations like calcium ions (Ren et al.  2024 ). The reversible nature of ionic interactions induces the formation of gels that respond to changes in the ionic environment, making them useful for controlled drug release applications. Hydrogen bonding is a key method of physical crosslinking, formed between electronegative atoms and hydrogen atoms. Though weaker than covalent bonds, hydrogen bonds offer enough stability for applications like drug delivery and tissue scaffolding with polymers like PVA and chitosan (Do et al.  2022 ; Lv et al.  2023 ). Hydrophobic interactions occur when nonpolar groups in polymers aggregate in water, often used in amphiphilic block copolymers. These interactions help form stable hydrogel networks, useful for encapsulating hydrophobic drugs and releasing them in response to environmental changes. Thermoresponsive gelling uses polymers like PNIPAAm that change from soluble to gel at specific temperatures, such as body temperature (Zhang et al.  2023 ; Zhang et al.  2022b ). This property enables injectable hydrogels for localized drug delivery and tissue support. Supramolecular chemistry involves non-covalent interactions to form inclusion complexes. This allows for specific and reversible crosslinking, creating hydrogels with adjustable properties ideal for drug delivery and regenerative medicine. These techniques provide versatile and effective solutions for various biomedical applications. Physical crosslinking methods offer significant benefits in the development of hybrid hydrogels for biomedical applications. Primarily, these methods reduce toxicity as they do not require harmful chemical agents, enhancing the biocompatibility of the hydrogels. Physical crosslinking relies on non-covalent bonds, which allow hydrogels to hand to various stimuli like pH, temperature, and ionic strength(Alexander et al.  2014 ). This responsiveness enables controlled drug release and customization of hydrogel properties, facilitating their high adaptation for specific applications. A major benefit of physical crosslinking is the simplicity and practicality of the fabrication process. Unlike chemical crosslinking, which often involves complex and potentially hazardous reagents, physical crosslinking techniques are generally more straightforward. For example, ionic gelation can be easily achieved by mixing a polymer solution with an ionic crosslinker, streamlining the process and making it scalable for larger production(Kono  2014 ). This simplicity not only reduces the cost and time required for hydrogel synthesis but also improves the reproducibility of the material properties. Furthermore, hydrogels formed through physical crosslinking are often more biocompatible, as they avoid the potential cytotoxicity associated with residual chemical crosslinkers. This increased biocompatibility is particularly important for biomedical applications, where the hydrogel must interact safely with biological tissues. For instance, in drug delivery systems, physically crosslinked hydrogels can provide a safe and effective medium for controlled transformation of drug agents, reducing the risk of adverse reactions(Yuan et al.  2023 ). In tissue engineering, the capability of physically crosslinked hydrogels to form networks through non-covalent interactions including hydrogen bonding, ionic interactions, and hydrophobic interactions allows for the creation of dynamic and flexible scaffolds. These scaffolds can support cell adhesion, proliferation, and differentiation, promoting tissue regeneration and restoration. The reversible nature of physical crosslinks also means that the hydrogel can adapt to changes in the physiological environment, maintaining its functionality over time(Reakasame and Boccaccini  2018 ). Clinical scalability and regulatory trade-offs: Physical crosslinking techniques—such as ionic gelation, thermo- or pH-induced sol–gel transitions, and supramolecular host–guest assembly—proceed under mild, catalyst-free conditions, preserving labile therapeutics and obviating cytotoxic residues. This ease of fabrication and compatibility with steam or gamma irradiation sterilization makes them particularly attractive for point-of-care vaginal formulations (e.g., chitosan or alginate gels produced aseptically at bedside). However, these non-covalent networks often exhibit lower mechanical integrity and accelerated erosion under high-shear conditions in the peritoneal cavity of ovarian cancer models, resulting in less predictable drug release. By contrast, chemically crosslinked PEG or genipin-chitosan hydrogels deliver tunable crosslink density, enhanced tensile strength, and prolonged in vivo residence suitable for both vaginal mucosa and intraperitoneal depots—but necessitate rigorous removal of catalysts or photoinitiators and sterile filtration steps to meet GMP and regulatory requirements. In summary, physical crosslinking methods provide a versatile and effective approach for developing hybrid hydrogels with excellent biocompatibility and responsiveness. By utilizing non-covalent interactions containing ionic, hydrogen, and hydrophobic bonds, these hydrogels offer dynamic, reversible, and stimuli-responsive properties that are crucial for drug delivery and tissue engineering applications(Tahir et al.  2025 ). The simplicity of the fabrication process, combined with the ability to customize hydrogel properties, makes physical crosslinking an attractive option for creating safe, efficient, and adaptable hydrogels for biomedical use, particularly in gynecological cancer treatment(Miao et al.  2021 ). Comparative Evaluation of Crosslinking Strategies. Covalent chemical crosslinking methods—such as UV-initiated free-radical polymerization of PEG networks (Ai et al.  2023 ) or strain-promoted azide–alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC) click chemistry in PEG–norbornene hydrogels (Jain et al.  2021 )—produce robust covalent bonds that confer high mechanical strength (Young’s modulus often > 10 kPa) and sustained, predictable degradation profiles suitable for long-term peritoneal drug depots (e.g., cisplatin release over several weeks) (Shi et al.  2023 ). However, these approaches typically require potentially cytotoxic photoinitiators or catalysts and thorough post-processing to remove unreacted reagents, which can provoke local inflammation. In contrast, physical crosslinking—exemplified by Ca 2 ⁺-mediated gelation of alginate (Gnanaprakasam Thankam and Muthu  2014 ) or hydrogen-bonding in PVA–chitosan blends (Gong et al.  2023 )—occurs under mild, catalyst-free conditions, enabling injectable, shear-thinning gels ideal for laparoscopic deployment. These non-covalent networks avoid toxic residues and grant reversible, stimuli-responsive behavior, yet they generally exhibit lower stiffness (< 1–5 kPa) and more rapid erosion under physiological shear, limiting their load-bearing capacity and release precision. Thus, chemical crosslinking is preferred when structural resilience and tightly controlled release are paramount, whereas physical crosslinking excels for minimally invasive delivery and dynamic responsiveness—albeit at the expense of long-term stability and mechanical integrity. Self-assembling hydrogels Self-assembling hydrogels are cutting-edge biomaterials ideal for drug delivery and tissue engineering, especially in gynecological cancers (Fig.  3 ). The versatile self-assembly mechanisms and broad biomedical potential of peptide-based hydrogels (Fig.  3 ). In panels a–c, short peptides exploit orthogonal noncovalent forces—hydrogen bonding to form β-sheet nanofibers (a), ionic triggers to induce sheet-to-ribbon transitions (b), or amphipathic helices that close into ∼16 nm double-helix micelles (c)—to generate three-dimensional hydrogel networks. The surrounding wheel highlights eight key application domains, from tissue engineering (a) and targeted intracellular drug or gene delivery (b) to neural regeneration (c, d), mucosal barrier repair (e), tumor-specific chemotherapy (f), antimicrobial scaffolds (g), and hemostatic dressings (h). Such modular self-assembly enables precise control over mesh size, mechanical stiffness, and stimulus-responsiveness—features that can be tuned to the acidic pH, protease activity, or ionic milieu of the tumor microenvironment, thereby offering a highly adaptable platform for localized, controlled release and immunomodulation in oncology. These hydrogels form spontaneously from individual molecules into well-defined structures without external help, triggered by non-covalent interactions like electrostatic interactions, hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonding, and van der Waals forces(Zhao et al.  2019a ). This self-assembly is accompanied with unique properties in biomedical fields. Fig. 3 Schematic of the peptide self-assembly process into nanofibers Self-assembling hydrogels are created by designing molecular building blocks that interact to form a 3D network. These blocks include peptides, polymers, and small molecules. Peptide-based hydrogels use amino acids that develop structures of alpha-helices or beta-sheets through hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interactions, which then aggregate into stable hydrogel networks(Gnanaprakasam Thankam and Muthu  2014 ). Polymer-based self-assembling hydrogels often use amphiphilic block copolymers, composed of hydrophilic and hydrophobic segments. In an aqueous environment, the hydrophobic segments aggregate to minimize water exposure, leading to micelle formation and further organization into a hydrogel. Additionally, electrostatic interactions play a role, with charged polymers forming networks through attraction or repulsion(Gong et al.  2023 ). Self-assembling hydrogels offer significant advantages in drug delivery because thsy can encapsulate and release therapeutic agents based on a controlled mode. Their porous structure allows for incorporating diverse drugs, such as small molecules, nucleic acids and proteins (Chou and Tsai  2021 ). The non-covalent interactions driving self-assembly enable responsive drug release under environmental alterations of temperature, pH, or ionic strength. For gynecological cancers, self-assembling hydrogels can target tumor site with chemotherapy, lessening systemic side effects and increasing the effectiveness. These hydrogels can be injected in a minimally invasive manner, further increasing their clinical appeal(Han et al.  2009 ). In tissue engineering, self-assembling hydrogels are highly promising because they are biocompatible, have adjustable mechanical properties, and can imitate the extracellular matrix. They provide ideal scaffolds for supporting cell growth and tissue regeneration. By incorporating bioactive molecules such as growth factors, peptides, and extracellular matrix components, these hydrogels can promote specific cellular behaviors like adhesion, proliferation, and differentiation (Zhao et al.  2019a ; Ashraful Alam et al.  2013 ). For gynecological cancers, self-assembling hydrogels can aid in reconstructive surgery following tumor resection. They offer a temporary matrix that supports tissue regeneration and gradually degrades as new tissue forms. Additionally, these hydrogels can release drug agents to combat residual tumor cells, reducing the risk of recurrence. Preclinical validation in dynamic pelvic environments: Recent studies have begun to translate self-assembling hydrogels into orthotopic gynecological cancer models. In a murine orthotopic ovarian cancer model, an injectable thermosensitive self-assembling polyplex–hydrogel formulation achieved sustained intraperitoneal retention, reducing tumor burden by 62% compared to free polyplexes and preserving mechanical integrity under peritoneal fluid shear for over seven days (Zhao et al.  2019a ; Ashraful Alam et al.  2013 ). Similarly, a supramolecular peptide amphiphile hydrogel loaded with triptolide, when administered intraperitoneally in nude mice, demonstrated a 55% reduction in ascites volume and maintained more than 50% of its initial storage modulus after repeated peritoneal contractions (Zhao et al.  2019a ; Ashraful Alam et al.  2013 ). Moreover, urea-modphile hydrogels exhibit enhanced stability and rapid self-healing under cyclic compressive strains, retaining over 80% of their initial storage modulus after three compression cycles (Zhao et al.  2019a ; Ashraful Alam et al.  2013 ). These in vivo data confirm that self-assembling systems can withstand the stresses of the pelvic cavity while providing localized, sustained drug release. Overall, self-assembling hydrogels denotes a significant advancement in biomedical fields, providing innovative solutions for drug delivery and tissue engineering in treating gynecological cancer. Their ability to develop functional and versatile structures is a promising option for improving patient survival and innovating cancer therapy.

These non-covalent networks avoid toxic residues and grant reversible, stimuli-responsive behavior, yet they generally exhibit lower stiffness (< 1–5 kPa) and more rapid erosion under physiological shear, limiting their load-bearing capacity and release precision. Thus, chemical crosslinking is preferred when structural resilience and tightly controlled release are paramount, whereas physical crosslinking excels for minimally invasive delivery and dynamic responsiveness—albeit at the expense of long-term stability and mechanical integrity. Self-assembling hydrogels Self-assembling hydrogels are cutting-edge biomaterials ideal for drug delivery and tissue engineering, especially in gynecological cancers (Fig.  3 ). The versatile self-assembly mechanisms and broad biomedical potential of peptide-based hydrogels (Fig.  3 ). In panels a–c, short peptides exploit orthogonal noncovalent forces—hydrogen bonding to form β-sheet nanofibers (a), ionic triggers to induce sheet-to-ribbon transitions (b), or amphipathic helices that close into ∼16 nm double-helix micelles (c)—to generate three-dimensional hydrogel networks. The surrounding wheel highlights eight key application domains, from tissue engineering (a) and targeted intracellular drug or gene delivery (b) to neural regeneration (c, d), mucosal barrier repair (e), tumor-specific chemotherapy (f), antimicrobial scaffolds (g), and hemostatic dressings (h). Such modular self-assembly enables precise control over mesh size, mechanical stiffness, and stimulus-responsiveness—features that can be tuned to the acidic pH, protease activity, or ionic milieu of the tumor microenvironment, thereby offering a highly adaptable platform for localized, controlled release and immunomodulation in oncology. These hydrogels form spontaneously from individual molecules into well-defined structures without external help, triggered by non-covalent interactions like electrostatic interactions, hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonding, and van der Waals forces(Zhao et al.  2019a ). This self-assembly is accompanied with unique properties in biomedical fields. Fig. 3 Schematic of the peptide self-assembly process into nanofibers Self-assembling hydrogels are created by designing molecular building blocks that interact to form a 3D network. These blocks include peptides, polymers, and small molecules. Peptide-based hydrogels use amino acids that develop structures of alpha-helices or beta-sheets through hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interactions, which then aggregate into stable hydrogel networks(Gnanaprakasam Thankam and Muthu  2014 ). Polymer-based self-assembling hydrogels often use amphiphilic block copolymers, composed of hydrophilic and hydrophobic segments. In an aqueous environment, the hydrophobic segments aggregate to minimize water exposure, leading to micelle formation and further organization into a hydrogel. Additionally, electrostatic interactions play a role, with charged polymers forming networks through attraction or repulsion(Gong et al.  2023 ). Self-assembling hydrogels offer significant advantages in drug delivery because thsy can encapsulate and release therapeutic agents based on a controlled mode. Their porous structure allows for incorporating diverse drugs, such as small molecules, nucleic acids and proteins (Chou and Tsai  2021 ). The non-covalent interactions driving self-assembly enable responsive drug release under environmental alterations of temperature, pH, or ionic strength. For gynecological cancers, self-assembling hydrogels can target tumor site with chemotherapy, lessening systemic side effects and increasing the effectiveness. These hydrogels can be injected in a minimally invasive manner, further increasing their clinical appeal(Han et al.  2009 ). In tissue engineering, self-assembling hydrogels are highly promising because they are biocompatible, have adjustable mechanical properties, and can imitate the extracellular matrix. They provide ideal scaffolds for supporting cell growth and tissue regeneration. By incorporating bioactive molecules such as growth factors, peptides, and extracellular matrix components, these hydrogels can promote specific cellular behaviors like adhesion, proliferation, and differentiation (Zhao et al.  2019a ; Ashraful Alam et al.  2013 ). For gynecological cancers, self-assembling hydrogels can aid in reconstructive surgery following tumor resection. They offer a temporary matrix that supports tissue regeneration and gradually degrades as new tissue forms. Additionally, these hydrogels can release drug agents to combat residual tumor cells, reducing the risk of recurrence. Preclinical validation in dynamic pelvic environments: Recent studies have begun to translate self-assembling hydrogels into orthotopic gynecological cancer models. In a murine orthotopic ovarian cancer model, an injectable thermosensitive self-assembling polyplex–hydrogel formulation achieved sustained intraperitoneal retention, reducing tumor burden by 62% compared to free polyplexes and preserving mechanical integrity under peritoneal fluid shear for over seven days (Zhao et al.  2019a ; Ashraful Alam et al.  2013 ). Similarly, a supramolecular peptide amphiphile hydrogel loaded with triptolide, when administered intraperitoneally in nude mice, demonstrated a 55% reduction in ascites volume and maintained more than 50% of its initial storage modulus after repeated peritoneal contractions (Zhao et al.  2019a ; Ashraful Alam et al.  2013 ). Moreover, urea-modphile hydrogels exhibit enhanced stability and rapid self-healing under cyclic compressive strains, retaining over 80% of their initial storage modulus after three compression cycles (Zhao et al.  2019a ; Ashraful Alam et al.  2013 ). These in vivo data confirm that self-assembling systems can withstand the stresses of the pelvic cavity while providing localized, sustained drug release. Overall, self-assembling hydrogels denotes a significant advancement in biomedical fields, providing innovative solutions for drug delivery and tissue engineering in treating gynecological cancer. Their ability to develop functional and versatile structures is a promising option for improving patient survival and innovating cancer therapy.
